questions.q: Which of these best matches this lesson's definition of data lineage?
options: The recorded path data takes from its origin, through every transformation, to where it's used
A backup copy of a database kept in a second data center
The total storage size a dataset occupies on disk
A list of every user who has ever logged into a system
questions.explain: Lineage is specifically about the path and the transformations along the way, not storage, backups, or access logs.

questions.q: Which four reasons does this lesson give for why organizations invest in lineage?
options: Trust, impact analysis, root cause analysis, and audit/regulatory requirements
Faster internet speeds, cheaper storage, better branding, and fewer meetings
Smaller file sizes, prettier dashboards, shorter onboarding, and less code
Higher sales, lower taxes, improved morale, and fewer servers
questions.explain: The lesson's four reasons are trust (knowing where a number came from), impact analysis (checking dependencies before a change), root cause analysis (tracing a problem backward), and satisfying audit/regulatory requirements.

questions.q: Which statement is an example of business lineage, per this lesson?
options: "Customer Lifetime Value on the executive dashboard comes from the CRM and the billing system"
"dbo.CLV_Summary.LifetimeValueUSD is computed in sp_CalculateCLV by summing Billing.Invoices.AmountPaid"
"The server has 64 gigabytes of RAM"
"The nightly job runs at 2 AM Eastern time"
questions.explain: Business lineage uses plain domain terms and system names, without specific tables, columns, or code â€” exactly the level a non-technical stakeholder needs.

questions.q: What does table-level lineage record, according to this lesson?
options: Which tables feed which other tables, without specifying which columns are involved
Which specific columns feed which specific columns
The total storage size of every table in a database
The names of every user who has queried a table
questions.explain: Table-level lineage is coarse â€” it shows a relationship between two tables as a whole, like 'stg.Orders_Clean feeds dw.FactSales,' without column detail.

questions.q: Which extraction method reads a database's own transaction log to capture every insert, update, and delete as a discrete, ordered event?
options: Change Data Capture (CDC)
Full extract
API pull
Flat file drop
questions.explain: CDC reads the transaction log directly, giving you the richest possible lineage â€” a row's full history of changes, not just its current state.

questions.q: In ETL, where does transformation happen relative to loading?
options: Before loading, in a dedicated transformation engine
After loading, inside the warehouse
Transformation never happens in ETL
At the exact same moment as extraction, with no separate step
questions.explain: ETL stands for Extract, Transform, Load â€” the transform step happens before the finished data is loaded into the warehouse.

questions.q: How do you open lineage view for a Power BI workspace?
options: From the workspace list view, open the View dropdown and select Lineage
It must be requested from Microsoft support
By exporting the workspace as a PDF
There is no way to view lineage inside Power BI itself
questions.explain: Lineage view is built into every workspace â€” accessed via the View dropdown's Lineage option, no setup required.

questions.q: What does a 'Certified' endorsement badge signal in Power BI, according to this lesson?
options: The content passed a more rigorous review, typically by a central BI or governance team â€” the strongest trust signal Power BI offers
The content has never been refreshed
The content is scheduled for deletion
The content is only visible to the original creator
questions.explain: Certified is described as the strongest endorsement level, usually set after review by a central governance team, distinct from the lighter 'Promoted' status.

questions.q: What does 'upstream' mean relative to a given dataset?
options: Everything that feeds it â€” the sources and transformations before it
Everything that consumes it â€” the reports built on top of it
Only the very first source system in the entire organization
Any dataset stored in the same database
questions.explain: Upstream is everything that feeds the dataset in question â€” its sources and the transformations data passed through to arrive there.

questions.q: What is a 'business rule' as described in this lesson?
options: Logic that encodes an organizational decision, embedded inside a transformation
A company's formal HR policy document
Any SQL statement regardless of what it does
A naming convention applied to table names
questions.explain: A business rule is the organizational decision behind the mechanics â€” e.g. which Discount field to use, or whether Revenue includes tax â€” tangled into the transformation's logic.

questions.q: What question does impact analysis answer?
options: If this changes, what breaks?
Where did this error originate?
Who is the technical owner of this dataset?
How much storage does this table consume?
questions.explain: Impact analysis is specifically about discovering the consequences of a proposed change before it's made.

questions.q: What are the four stages of a change impact assessment, in order, per this lesson?
options: Propose, trace lineage, classify risk, sign off and communicate
Deploy, monitor, rollback, document
Design, build, test, deploy
Trace lineage, propose, deploy, review
questions.explain: The change is proposed precisely, lineage is traced and documented, the findings are risk-classified, and then the change is approved and communicated to affected owners before shipping.

questions.q: What three things does this lesson say good lineage documentation should capture for every dependency?
options: Nodes, edges, and ownership
File size, row count, and creation date
Server IP address, port number, and protocol
Only the names of the two datasets involved
questions.explain: Nodes (the datasets/fields/reports), edges (the dependency and its transformation), and ownership (who's responsible for each side) are the three things worth recording.

questions.q: In the visual conventions this lesson describes, what does an arrow in a lineage diagram represent?
options: The direction of data flow, from upstream to downstream
The physical distance between two servers
The number of rows in a table
The seniority of the dataset's owner
questions.explain: Arrows point from upstream to downstream, the same convention used in text form throughout this chapter since Lesson 12.

questions.q: What approach does this lesson say most mature lineage practices actually land on?
options: A hybrid: automated lineage as the backbone for parseable pipeline code, plus manual documentation to fill the gaps automation can't reach
Exclusively manual documentation, since automation is never worth the investment
Exclusively automated lineage, since manual documentation is never useful
No lineage documentation at all, relying entirely on institutional memory
questions.explain: Neither approach alone solves the whole problem â€” automation covers what it can scan, and manual documentation covers the tribal-knowledge and off-pipeline steps it can't.

questions.q: Which of these is an enterprise platform this lesson names that combines a data catalog with automated lineage capture?
options: Microsoft Purview
OpenLineage
The LTV Academy course outline
A plain text wiki page
questions.explain: Microsoft Purview scans an organization's data estate and automatically builds a lineage map from what it finds, alongside Collibra and Alation as similar enterprise platforms.

questions.q: What was the actual root cause the analyst found when tracing the lineage at the column level?
options: A filter condition meant to exclude voided transactions was also excluding legitimate after-hours sales, due to a POS-side labeling change
The warehouse table ran out of storage space
The dashboard was reading from the wrong year's data entirely
A currency conversion rate was outdated
questions.explain: A recent change to how the POS system tagged transactions caused legitimate late sales to be excluded by a filter that was only supposed to remove voided transactions.

questions.q: What specifically caused the same real customer to appear as multiple rows in the unified customer view?
options: The merge logic matched records by email address, and slightly different formatting of the same email caused mismatches
The unified view intentionally duplicates every customer for backup purposes
Customers were asked to register twice on purpose
The CRM system deleted all customer records every night
questions.explain: Formatting differences like J.Smith@email.com versus j.smith@email.com for the same person caused the matching logic to treat them as different customers.

questions.q: What is the main practical skill this lab lesson is meant to build?
options: Tracing a lineage path by hand, performing impact analysis before a change, and using lineage to decide where to look first when something breaks
Writing production-grade ETL code in a specific programming language
Memorizing the exact table names used at one specific real company
Designing a company's entire database schema from scratch
questions.explain: The lab is explicitly hands-on and tool-free, focused on the transferable skill of tracing, impact-checking, and root-causing using a lineage path, not on any specific software or real company's schema.

questions.q: What single habit does this lesson identify as common to all three of this chapter's case studies, and as the fix that would have caught each problem earlier?
options: Checking what's downstream before assuming an upstream change is fine
Always rewriting a pipeline from scratch after any bug is found
Never allowing more than one system to store customer data
Switching every report to real-time data instead of batch processing
questions.explain: Each case study involved an upstream change silently breaking an unwritten downstream assumption; checking downstream impact before trusting an upstream change is the habit that catches this earlier.
